asien-altertum#sections.0.paragraphs.2: In Persia the Sasanian kings ruled as Kings of Kings over a multi-ethnic empire in which the nobility, the Zoroastrian priests, and the warriors were separated by estate. Their permanent conflict with Rome and Byzantium over Armenia and Mesopotamia so exhausted both sides in the 7th century that the Arab armies had an easy task. In India, by contrast, great empires such as the Maurya, the Gupta, and the Chola remained exceptions; mostly numerous regional kings shared power, though the Chola in the south also ruled across the sea with a fleet.
asien-altertum#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
asien-altertum#sections.1.paragraphs.0: The great majority of people lived in the countryside from growing rice and millet. In China the family, headed by the father, stood at the centre, and the veneration of ancestors connected the living with the dead. The state demanded from the peasants taxes in grain and cloth as well as labour service, with which walls, canals, and palaces were built. Those who could no longer render these dues fled or joined revolts, which several times brought down entire dynasties.
asien-altertum#sections.1.paragraphs.1: In India the caste system ordered society by birth into priests, warriors, peasants and merchants, and servants; below them stood the so-called untouchables. Buddhists and Jains rejected this order of rank, and in the monasteries people of all origins lived together. Women in the early civilizations of Asia mostly had limited rights, but there were exceptions: Buddhist nuns, learned ladies-in-waiting in Japan, and rulers such as Wu Zetian show that education and power were not reserved for men alone.
asien-altertum#sections.1.paragraphs.2: The cities of Asia far surpassed those of Europe in size. Chang'an, the capital of the Tang, was laid out on a grid, surrounded by walls, and divided into quarters with a night-time curfew; in its two great markets Persians, Sogdians, Indians, and Arabs traded. Teahouses, theatres, and temple festivals shaped city life, and with tea, which became the popular drink under the Tang, a distinct culture of enjoyment arose.
asien-altertum#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
asien-altertum#sections.2.paragraphs.0: Alongside Confucianism, Daoism arose in China, the way of non-action in harmony with nature ascribed to Laozi. The two teachings complemented each other: an official was a Confucian while in office and a Daoist in retirement. Buddhism was added by way of the Silk Road and became the third great teaching through monasteries, cave temples such as Longmen and Dunhuang, and pilgrims such as Xuanzang, who brought Indian scriptures to China. From China it spread to Korea and, in the 6th century, to Japan.
asien-altertum#sections.2.paragraphs.1: Persia was the home of Zoroastrianism with its struggle between good and evil, which influenced Christianity, Judaism, and Islam. Under the Sasanians the teaching of Zarathustra became the state religion; at the same time Jews, Christians, and Manichaeans lived in the empire, and the academy of Gundeshapur collected Greek and Indian knowledge. In India Sanskrit poetry, astronomy, and mathematics flourished; the dramas of Kalidasa and the calculations of Aryabhata are among the high points of the Gupta period.
asien-altertum#sections.2.paragraphs.2: In China historical writing attained a standing under Sima Qian that it had nowhere else in antiquity: every dynasty had the history of its predecessor written, and the archives of the court reach back to the Han period. The invention of woodblock printing in the 7th or 8th century made Buddhist sutras, calendars, and later the Confucian classics available in large numbers. In Japan ladies-in-waiting such as Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shonagon created new literary forms, the novel and the diary, in the Japanese syllabic script.
asien-altertum#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
asien-altertum#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The Silk Road was not a single route but a network of caravan routes and sea lanes connecting China, India, Persia, and the Mediterranean. Silk, lacquer, porcelain, and paper travelled westwards, and glass, horses, spices, precious stones, and silver eastwards; intermediaries such as the Sogdians in Samarkand and the Kushan Empire in Central Asia grew rich. Religions, diseases, and inventions travelled with the goods, and the harbours of southern India and Southeast Asia linked the network with maritime trade across the Indian Ocean.
asien-altertum#sections.3.paragraphs.1: For centuries China was the technically leading region of the world. Cast iron, the wheelbarrow, the stirrup, the seismograph, paper, the compass, and woodblock printing originated here long before Europe. Under the Song dynasty gunpowder weapons, paper money, movable type, and huge blast furnaces were added, and Kaifeng became a city of a million people with trading companies and exchange houses. The Chinese built canals such as the Grand Canal, which connected northern and southern China and secured the rice supply of the capitals.
asien-altertum#sections.3.paragraphs.2: India exported cotton fabrics, pepper, and precious stones and received Roman gold in return, as thousands of coin finds in the south attest. Steel production in southern India supplied the famous wootz steel, from which Damascus blades were later forged. Persia controlled the trade between East and West, minted silver coins that reached as far as China and Scandinavia, and developed an irrigation technique with underground channels, the qanats, that is still in use today.
afrikanische-reiche#summary: From Aksum and Nubia through Mali, Songhai and Benin to Asante, Sokoto and the Zulu, Africa saw the rise of kingdoms, trading cities and centers of learning that were connected to the wider world across the Sahara, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic.
afrikanische-reiche#overview.0: In the centuries between antiquity and the colonial conquest, Africa was not a continent without history but a space of numerous states, cities and cultures. In the northeast, Aksum in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea rose to become a trading power on the Red Sea, minted its own coins and adopted Christianity in the 4th century under King Ezana. On the Nile stood the Christian kingdoms of Nubia, of which Makuria withstood the Arab armies in 652 and concluded a treaty with Egypt that remained in force for centuries.
afrikanische-reiche#overview.1: In West Africa, trade across the Sahara linked the goldfields on the upper Niger and Senegal with North Africa and the Mediterranean. On this basis the great empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai arose one after the other, their rulers controlling gold, salt and caravan routes. Mansa Musa made Mali famous throughout the Islamic world with his pilgrimage in 1324, and Timbuktu, with its mosques and manuscripts, became a center of Islamic scholarship. Further east lay Kanem-Bornu on Lake Chad and the city-states of the Hausa, while in the forest zone further south stood the Yoruba cities of Ife and Oyo and the kingdom of Benin with its famous metal art.
afrikanische-reiche#overview.2: On the coast of the Indian Ocean, between Somalia and Mozambique, the Swahili culture developed with trading cities such as Kilwa, Mombasa and later Zanzibar, which supplied gold, ivory and slaves to Arabia, India and China. In the interior of southern Africa, the ancestors of the Shona built the stone city of Great Zimbabwe, which was followed by the empire of Mutapa. In Ethiopia the Zagwe kings created the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, and from 1270 the Solomonic dynasty claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.
afrikanische-reiche#overview.3: From the late 15th century, contact with Portugal and other European powers changed the situation on the Atlantic coast. In the kingdom of Kongo the kings were baptized and sought an alliance with Lisbon, but saw the slave trade undermine their rule. African states such as Dahomey, Oyo and Asante took part in the trade in captives and acquired firearms and goods in return, while female rulers such as Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted the Portuguese for decades. By the 19th century more than twelve million people had been carried off across the Atlantic.
afrikanische-reiche#overview.4: In the 19th century new large states emerged once more: the Sokoto Caliphate grew out of the reform movement of Usman dan Fodio, Shaka shaped the Zulu kingdom, and the Merina kings united most of Madagascar. Wars and migrations in southern Africa, known as the Mfecane, redrew the political map. Many of these states were still independent around 1880; only with the Scramble for Africa did almost all of them lose their independence.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.0: The precolonial kingdoms refute the image, long widespread in Europe, of an Africa without history, states or written culture; monuments such as Great Zimbabwe and Lalibela and the manuscripts of Timbuktu are now part of the world heritage.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.1: Islam and Christianity spread along trade routes and through royal courts into large parts of Africa and still shape religion, law and education from the Sahel to Ethiopia.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.2: The Atlantic slave trade depopulated entire regions, intensified wars between African states and gave rise to the African diaspora in the Americas, with profound consequences up to the present.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.3: Many present-day states such as Ghana, Mali, Benin or Zimbabwe deliberately bear the names of precolonial kingdoms and invoke their heritage.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.4: Works of art such as the bronzes of Ife and Benin influenced modern European art; their return from European museums is still being negotiated today.
afrikanische-reiche#consequences.5: The wars and state foundations of the 19th century, such as the Zulu kingdom, Lesotho and the Sokoto Caliphate, had a lasting influence on political boundaries and identities in southern and western Africa.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.0: Around 330 King Ezana of Aksum converts to Christianity; Ethiopia becomes one of the oldest Christian countries in the world.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.1: In 652 the Nubian kingdom of Makuria concludes the Baqt treaty with Arab Egypt, which remains in force for about 600 years.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.2: Around 1235 Sundiata Keita founds the Mali Empire with his victory at Kirina; in 1324 Mansa Musa's pilgrimage makes Mali world-famous.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.3: Around 1200 the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are created; in 1270 the Solomonic dynasty begins in Ethiopia.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.4: In 1526 King Afonso I of Kongo complains in letters to Portugal that traders are carrying off free people.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.5: In 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms destroys the Songhai Empire at Tondibi.
afrikanische-reiche#keyFacts.6: In 1804 Usman dan Fodio begins the jihad from which the Sokoto Caliphate emerges; in 1816 Shaka takes over rule of the Zulu.
afrikanische-reiche#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
afrikanische-reiche#sections.0.paragraph: African kingdoms were organized in very different ways. Alongside centralized monarchies such as Benin, Asante or Dahomey there were loose federations of tributary princes such as Mali and Songhai, city-states such as the Hausa cities or the Swahili ports, and societies without any kings at all. The power of the great empires often rested less on fixed borders than on control over people, trade routes and tribute. Rulers bore titles such as mansa in Mali, askia in Songhai, oba in Benin, asantehene in Asante or negus in Ethiopia.

Many kings combined political and religious authority. The oba of Benin and the alaafin of Oyo were regarded as sacred persons who rarely appeared in public, while Muslim rulers in Mali, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu or Kano strengthened their position through pilgrimages to Mecca, scholars at court and Islamic law. In Ethiopia the Solomonic dynasty relied on the legend of its descent from King Solomon and on the church. At the same time councils such as the Oyo Mesi or the elders of Asante limited the power of the kings.

Wars decided the rise and fall of empires. Sundiata defeated the Sosso around 1235, Sunni Ali conquered the cities on the Niger for Songhai, and a Moroccan army with firearms destroyed the Songhai Empire in 1591. Firearms, which entered the region through the Saharan and Atlantic trade, shifted the balance of power; states such as Bornu, Dahomey and Asante built strong armies with them, while Oyo relied on its cavalry.

For a long time African rulers negotiated with the Europeans as equals. The kings of Kongo exchanged envoys with Portugal and the pope, Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba alternated between war, diplomacy and alliances with the Dutch, and the Merina kings of Madagascar concluded treaties with Britain. Only in the 19th century did European pressure grow so strong that states such as Ethiopia under Tewodros II or the Zulu kingdom were drawn into open wars with Britain.
afrikanische-reiche#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
afrikanische-reiche#sections.1.paragraph: The great majority of people lived as farmers, herders or fishermen in villages led by kinship groups and elders. Millet, sorghum, yams and rice, and in East Africa also bananas, formed the basis of their diet; cattle were a sign of wealth and prestige, especially in the south and east. Because land was usually plentiful but labor scarce, power was measured above all by the number of people who followed a ruler or the head of a family.

Many societies had hereditary occupational groups such as smiths, weavers or griots, who served at the courts as singers and keepers of history. Slavery was widespread in numerous African states, but it often differed from the plantation slavery of the Americas: unfree people worked as farmers, soldiers, servants or even officials, and their descendants could be absorbed into the families of their masters. The Atlantic slave trade, however, intensified kidnapping and warfare and turned captives into a commodity on a previously unknown scale.

Women played a visible role in many African societies. Queen mothers such as the iyoba in Benin or the asantehemaa in Asante had their own courts and political influence, and female rulers such as Njinga or Ranavalona I governed in their own right. Market women dominated the markets of West Africa, in Dahomey female warriors formed a unit of their own, and the scholar Nana Asma'u organized education for women in the Sokoto Caliphate.

Cities such as Timbuktu, Djenné, Kano, Kilwa, Benin or Kumasi were densely populated centers with markets, palaces and places of worship. Travellers such as Ibn Battuta described the security, prosperity and strict order of Mali, and Portuguese visitors compared Benin with European cities. Here merchants from North Africa, Arabia and India met local traders, and mixed cultures such as that of the Swahili emerged.
afrikanische-reiche#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
afrikanische-reiche#sections.2.paragraph: Alongside indigenous religions, which venerated ancestors, the forces of nature and a creator god, Christianity and Islam spread. Aksum and the kingdoms of Nubia became Christian as early as the 4th to 6th centuries, and the Ethiopian church developed a distinctive tradition with Ge'ez as its liturgical language, its own saints and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. Islam came to the Sahel through merchants from North Africa and to the east coast through the seafaring traders of the Indian Ocean, and was at first adopted mainly by rulers and traders.

Writing and scholarship were far more widespread than European observers later claimed. In Ethiopia chronicles and religious works were written in Ge'ez; in Timbuktu, Djenné and Kano scholars such as Ahmad Baba taught law, theology, grammar and astronomy, and libraries collected tens of thousands of manuscripts. Poems, chronicles and textbooks were composed in Arabic, but also in African languages such as Hausa or Swahili written in Arabic script.

Where writing was not used, storytellers and griots preserved history in oral tradition. The epic of Sundiata, which is still performed in West Africa today, tells of the founding of Mali and is an important historical source. King lists, praise songs and proverbs carried knowledge across generations and at the same time served to legitimize rulers.

The art of the African kingdoms reached a high level. In Ife, naturalistic heads of copper alloy and terracotta were made between the 12th and 15th centuries, and in Benin guilds of casters created relief plaques and commemorative heads for the court. Earthen buildings such as the mosques of Djenné and Timbuktu, the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe and the palaces of Kilwa bear witness to sophisticated architecture.
afrikanische-reiche#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
afrikanische-reiche#sections.3.paragraph: The economy of the great empires rested on long-distance trade. After the introduction of the camel, caravans crossed the Sahara, exchanging gold, ivory and slaves from the south for salt, copper, horses, cloth and books from the north. Until the discovery of the Americas, a large share of the gold circulating in the Mediterranean world and in Europe came from West Africa.

On the east coast the monsoon trade linked the Swahili cities with Arabia, Persia, India and China. Gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached the markets of the Indian Ocean through Sofala and Kilwa, and in return cotton textiles, glass beads and porcelain came to Africa. In the 19th century the Sultanate of Zanzibar built up clove plantations worked by enslaved people and controlled the ivory and slave trade deep into the interior of the continent.

Ironworking had been known in large parts of Africa for centuries; smiths made hoes, weapons and tools and often enjoyed special prestige. Weavers in Kano and elsewhere produced cotton cloth that was dyed with indigo and traded over long distances. Cowrie shells, gold dust, salt bars and pieces of copper served as currency in different regions.

With the Atlantic trade, commercial flows shifted to the coast. European traders supplied firearms, textiles, metal goods, spirits and cowrie shells and above all bought captives. For some coastal states this trade brought wealth and military strength, but it weakened the population and diverted the economy away from its own production. After Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, palm oil, groundnuts and ivory gained importance as exports.
mittelalter#summary: Between the end of Rome and the discovery of America, Christianity, feudalism, knights, monasteries, and rising cities shaped a new Europe, while the Mongols, Mali, and the Aztecs established great empires of their own.
mittelalter#overview.0: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Germanic kingdoms arose on its soil. The most successful were the Franks: their king Clovis was baptized a Catholic around 498 and thereby won the support of the church and of the Romance population. Charlemagne extended the Frankish kingdom as far as Saxony, Italy, and Spain and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800; his reign is regarded as the birth of medieval Europe.
mittelalter#overview.1: The High Middle Ages from the 11th to the 13th century were a period of growth. The population increased, forests were cleared, cities were founded, and cathedrals were built. Society was divided into estates: the nobility fought, the clergy prayed, the peasants worked. Through feudalism the king bound dukes and counts to himself, and they owed him loyalty and military service in return. Monasteries preserved the knowledge of antiquity, and from 1088 the first universities arose in Bologna, Paris, and Oxford.
mittelalter#overview.2: The Crusades from 1096 brought Europe into close and often violent contact with the Islamic world, but also promoted trade and the exchange of knowledge. From 793 the Vikings from Scandinavia plundered monasteries and coasts, founded cities such as Dublin and Kiev, and reached Greenland and North America. Their descendants, the Normans, conquered England in 1066. With the Magna Carta of 1215 kings had for the first time to acknowledge the rights of their subjects in writing.
mittelalter#overview.3: Powerful empires arose outside Europe as well: from 1206 Genghis Khan created the largest contiguous land empire in history, which allowed merchants such as Marco Polo to travel as far as China. In Mali in West Africa the gold-rich king Mansa Musa impressed the entire Islamic world on his pilgrimage in 1324, and in Mexico the Aztecs founded their capital Tenochtitlan around 1325.
mittelalter#overview.4: The Late Middle Ages were marked by crises. From 1347 the Black Death killed about a third of the European population, the Hundred Years' War devastated France, and famines and revolts shook the established order. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. At the same time printing, long-distance trade, and a new interest in antiquity were already announcing the modern age.
mittelalter#consequences.0: Christianity and the church shaped the law, education, calendar, and everyday life of Europe into the modern age; monasteries and universities became centres of knowledge.
mittelalter#consequences.1: France and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the Frankish kingdom, and many of today's European states, cities, and borders have medieval roots.
mittelalter#consequences.2: The Magna Carta and municipal charters established the idea that rulers too are bound by laws; out of this parliaments and civil rights developed.
mittelalter#consequences.3: The Crusades, the Mongol Empire, and long-distance trade connected Europe with Asia and Africa and carried knowledge, goods, and diseases such as the plague across continents.
mittelalter#consequences.4: The crises of the 14th century weakened the nobility and serfdom, strengthened the cities and wage labour, and prepared the ground for the Renaissance and the Reformation.
mittelalter#keyFacts.0: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founds the monastery of Monte Cassino; his rule shapes Western monasticism.
mittelalter#keyFacts.1: In 537 the emperor Justinian consecrates the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years.
mittelalter#keyFacts.2: In 843 the Treaty of Verdun divides the Frankish kingdom; out of West and East Francia arise France and Germany.
mittelalter#keyFacts.3: In 1077 King Henry IV asks the pope for forgiveness at Canossa: the climax of the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope.
mittelalter#keyFacts.4: In 1088 the first university in Europe is founded in Bologna, and around 1140 Saint-Denis becomes the first Gothic church.
mittelalter#keyFacts.5: From about 1200 to 1450 Great Zimbabwe flourishes in southern Africa; from 1438 Pachacuti builds up the Inca Empire in the Andes.
mittelalter#keyFacts.6: In 1356 the Hanseatic cities meet in Lübeck for the first Hanseatic Diet; in 1381 the great Peasants' Revolt breaks out in England.
mittelalter#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
mittelalter#sections.0.paragraphs.0: Medieval kings did not rule from a capital but travelled with their court from palatinate to palatinate and from monastery to monastery in order to show their presence in the land. Their power rested on feudalism: the king granted land and offices to dukes, counts, and bishops, who owed him loyalty, counsel, and military service in return and who in turn passed land on to knights. In the eastern part of the Frankish kingdom the dukes elected the king from 911 onwards, and with Otto I an imperial office arose that understood itself as the successor of Rome and of Charlemagne and that used the bishops as a support of its rule.
mittelalter#sections.0.paragraphs.1: The dispute over who was entitled to appoint bishops led in the 11th century to the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope, which was only partly settled by Henry IV's penitential journey to Canossa in 1077 and the Concordat of Worms in 1122. From then on the popes claimed supremacy over all rulers, called for crusades, and waged a struggle over Italy lasting decades with the Hohenstaufen such as Frederick II. In the Holy Roman Empire the princes thereby gained in independence, while in France and England the kings centralized their power.
mittelalter#sections.0.paragraphs.2: Outside Europe empires took other paths: under Justinian the Byzantine imperial office combined Roman law, the Greek language, and the Orthodox faith; in 988, with the baptism of Vladimir, Kievan Rus adopted Christianity and writing from Byzantium. In the Andes the Inca under Pachacuti created a state that administered millions of people without writing or wheels, by means of roads, storehouses, and knotted cords. In Africa rulers such as those of Great Zimbabwe and Mali controlled the trade in gold and ivory and built their power upon it.
mittelalter#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
mittelalter#sections.1.paragraphs.0: About nine out of ten people lived as peasants, many of them as serfs who paid dues to the lord of the manor and performed compulsory labour. Village life followed the church year and the seasons; from the 11th century the three-field system, the heavy wheeled plough, and the horse collar for draught horses increased yields. Crop failures nevertheless led again and again to famines, and life expectancy was far below that of today. After the Black Death labour became scarce, and peasants demanded freedom and better conditions, as in England in 1381.
mittelalter#sections.1.paragraphs.1: In the cities a new society of merchants, craftsmen, and day labourers arose, who escaped serfdom after a year according to the principle that city air makes you free. Guilds regulated the training, prices, and quality of the crafts, and the city council, usually dominated by rich merchant families, negotiated with kings and princes. Women ran workshops and shops, worked in the textile and brewing trades, and in cities such as Cologne even appeared as guilds of their own. Jews lived in separate quarters, were excluded from the crafts, and were repeatedly exposed to persecution.
mittelalter#sections.1.paragraphs.2: The nobility lived in castles and defined itself through arms, hunting, and the tournament; the ideal of the knight combined bravery with piety and courtly manners. At courts such as that of Eleanor of Aquitaine, troubadours and minnesingers sang of love and created a poetry in the vernacular languages. Monasteries took in the sons and daughters of the nobility, cared for the sick and the poor, and offered women such as Hildegard of Bingen a space for education and influence.
mittelalter#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
mittelalter#sections.2.paragraphs.0: The church pervaded every sphere of life: baptism, marriage, and burial, feast days, fasting, and the tithe determined the year, and the fear of hell and purgatory shaped people's thinking. The Rule of Benedict made monasteries places of prayer, work, and learning, whose scriptoria copied the texts of antiquity. In the 13th century Franciscans and Dominicans entered the cities and preached poverty, while pilgrims travelled to Santiago, Rome, and Jerusalem and relics were venerated. Byzantium and Kiev followed the Orthodox faith, which separated definitively from Rome in 1054.
mittelalter#sections.2.paragraphs.1: With the universities of Bologna, Paris, and Oxford, a new type of place of learning arose from the 11th century onwards, in which law, theology, medicine, and the seven liberal arts were taught. Scholasticism sought to ground faith in reason; to this end Thomas Aquinas combined the philosophy of Aristotle, rediscovered through Arabic translations, with Christian doctrine. At the same time poetry flourished in the vernacular languages, from the Nibelungenlied through Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival to Dante's Divine Comedy.
mittelalter#sections.2.paragraphs.2: Architecture reflected this new departure: the massive Romanesque churches with thick walls were followed from 1140 by the Gothic cathedrals, whose pointed arches, buttresses, and coloured glass windows let light into the interior as an image of God. Music was written down in notation for the first time, and polyphony developed in Paris. Outside Europe the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised walls metres high without mortar, and in Cusco and Machu Picchu the Inca fitted stones together so precisely that no knife blade fits between them.
mittelalter#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
mittelalter#sections.3.paragraphs.0: From the 11th to the 13th century the population of Europe doubled; forests were cleared, marshes drained, and settlers recruited as far as Eastern Europe. Water mills and windmills replaced manual labour in grinding, fulling, and sawing, and in the mines of the Harz and the Ore Mountains silver was extracted, which set coinage going again. Fairs in Champagne and later in Frankfurt and Geneva connected the merchants of Italy with those of Flanders and Germany.
mittelalter#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Long-distance trade organized itself in leagues: around 1356 the Hanseatic League linked some 200 cities from London to Novgorod and traded in cloth, furs, wax, herring, and salt on its rounded cogs. Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa dominated Mediterranean trade in spices and silk from the East and developed bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and banks; the church forbade interest, but the merchants found ways to circumvent this prohibition. In Africa, caravans across the Sahara and harbours on the Swahili coast connected goldfields and sources of ivory with Cairo, India, and China.
